summary: Analog sites, whose terrain resembles the Moon and Mars, are used on Earth to prepare for missions to these bodies. However, existing studies focus on a few well-known regions, and because Moon, Mars and Earth data sit in separate sources, comparing locations with the same criteria requires expertise. This study aims to let anyone identify Earth locations that resemble Shackleton crater on the Moon and Jezero crater on Mars, and to compare their similarities and differences using NASA data. The research question is how the degree of terrain similarity to these craters, and where a location differs, can be shown in an understandable way. To this end, the SPACE SYNC simulation and analysis platform was developed. It uses NASADEM, LOLA, CTX DTM, MODIS, Diviner, NASA POWER and NASA GIBS data, calculates slope, height difference and roughness for a 10×10 km area around a selected point, presents them beside the Moon and Mars references, and expresses similarity with a difference number (D). Its Explore, Compare and My places sections end in a scientific report output. A solo and multiplayer mission simulation also lets users play and compare a mission in a Moon or Mars crater with its analog arena on Earth. The study is limited by data resolution and analysis area; atmosphere, gravity and radiation are excluded from the comparison. The platform aims to make analog site research accessible to everyone, from students to researchers.
details: Space Sync is a web platform that helps find places on Earth whose terrain resembles the Shackleton crater on the Moon and the Jezero crater on Mars, and shows both the similarity and the difference in a measurable way using NASA data. When a user clicks a point on the map or globe, the system instantly downloads the elevation data for the 10×10 km area around that point. From this data it calculates slope, elevation range and roughness, presents them side by side with Moon and Mars references, and expresses the similarity as a difference score (D). The platform lets users compare two locations on three-dimensional terrain generated from real elevation data and obtain the results as a scientific report. Its intended impact is to turn analog site research from a task reserved for specialists into an experience anyone can use, from students to researchers, and to make less-studied and potentially more suitable locations visible. The project was built with openly accessible NASA data such as NASADEM, LOLA, CTX DTM, MODIS, Diviner, NASA POWER and NASA GIBS, together with AWS Terrain Tiles and OpenStreetMap; the data processing pipeline was built with Python 3.12 (rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, GeoPandas, PyArrow), and the interface was written in JavaScript, React and Vite. The map and globe views are rendered with MapLibre GL and Three.js (WebGL), and the three-dimensional terrain scene generated from real elevation data is drawn with Three.js. The code was written on Windows, versioned with Git and GitHub, and published as a serverless, static site on GitHub Pages through GitHub Actions. The project is creative in combining scientific comparison with an arcade-style mission simulation. In this simulation, one player works in a mission area on the Moon or Mars while the other works on Earth in an analog arena with similar terrain, and at the end of the mission the similarities and differences between the two environments are compared. In our design process, our team prioritized honesty and accessibility. No numbers were fabricated, and metrics with no data were marked “Data missing” instead of being shown as zero. Factors that cannot be compared, such as atmosphere, gravity and radiation, are always kept visible, and it is stated clearly that the method could not be validated in a positive control. In the simulation, real measurements are kept separate from game rules, and the interface was designed in plain language so that everyone can use it.
